The remanence in extrusive volcanic rocks of Lower Carboniferous (Visean) age in the Pennines of central England has been reinvestigated, employing detailed thermal demagnetisation and incorporating new geological knowledge of field relationships. Indications of primary remanence identified by early studies are supported and four successive reversals in the Asbian- Brigantian succession (about 335 Ma) reeognised. A mean (reversed) direction of D/I = 203/36 ° (10 sites, R = 9.75) yields a pole position at 336°E 14°S (dp/dm ~ 6/10°). nics of the Derby- shire Dome in the Pennine Hills of central En- gland. The results are summarised in Table 1. They include investigations (Belshr, 1957; Clegg et al., 1957) made before cleaning methods were routinely employed. Subsequent studies (Everitt and Belshr, 1960) found evidence for primary remanence and ancient field reversal. The axis of remanence was oriented NE -/SW + contrasting with the typical southerly shallow-directed rema- nences in most other European Carboniferous rocks. Later unpublished studies include more ex- tensive sampling and alternating field (a.f.) de- magnetisation (Titman, 1971; Moyse, 1973)and thermal demagnetisation (Titman, 1971). They also recognised reversals of magnetisation and direc- tions divergent from remanence in contempora- neous limestones in northern England (Turner and Tarling, 1975; Turner et al., 1979). Unfortunately, both Titman and Moyse experi- enced difficulties in differentiating between lavas and intrusions and were not able to take ad- vantage of recent geological investigations (In- stitute of Geological Sciences, 1969, 1970, 1975a,b, 1976a,b, 1977a,b; Waiters and Ineson, 1981) clarifying the nature and stratigraphic position of outcrops in these poorly exposed rocks. in contempora- neous limestones in northern England (Turner and Tarling, 1975; Turner et al., 1979). Unfortunately, both Titman and Moyse experi- enced difficulties in differentiating between lavas and intrusions and were not able to take ad- vantage of recent geological investigations (In- stitute of Geological Sciences, 1969, 1970, 1975a,b, 1976a,b, 1977a,b; Waiters and Ineson, 1981) clarifying the nature and stratigraphic position of outcrops in these poorly exposed rocks. The pre- sent study has been undertaken to exploit this knowledge and resolve the nature of magnetic remanence by employing modern techniques of stepwise thermal demagnetisation and component analysis. It supplements study of six units in this area by Rolph (1984) published in Rolph and Shaw (1985) and undertaken to derive estimates of the palaeointensity of the Lower Carboniferous geomagnetic field. 2. Geological outline The lavas are interleaved with marine shelf limestones belonging to the Tournasian and Visean epochs of the Dinantian Subsystem of the Silesian System. The limestones attain a total thickness of 660 m in this area (Cope, 1973; Dunham, 1973). They are succeeeded by a deltaic infill to the marine basin (the Millstone Grit Series) assigned TABLE 1 Summary of previous palaeomagnetic inve

n sampled at seven sites (Table 2), one on each of the exposed bodies. Up to 18 separate cores were drilled at each site with portable two-stroke drills and oriented in situ by sights on the Sun and magnetic bearings linked to topographic sites. In the laboratory cores were sliced into 2.4 cm long cylinders and measured by 'Minispin' magnetometers. Although a.f. demag- netisation was undertaken, this method only prop- erly recovered the component structure when a viscous overprint was the single addition to the characteristic remanence; at many sites a history of partial ancient secondary overprinting could only be recognised by thermal demagnetisation. Accordingly, only this method of treatment was pursued and all results discussed here are based on it. Steps of 100°C to 300°C, 100°C or 50°C to 500°C, and then in 20°C steps to 600°C were employed, or higher if a coherent component re- mained at this stage. Susceptibility measurements were used to monitor changes in the magnetic mineralogy during progressive cleaning. Following initial study of directional stereoplots, the compo- nent structure was resolved by study of orthogonal vector plots and principal component analysis. 3.2. dies yield two contrasting directions of magnetisation: in the central part of the Derbyshire pericline mixed polarity directions (mean D/I = 211/37 ° (4 sites, R = 3.92)) comparable to the lavas imply a Lower Carboniferous age of emplacement; in the SE Upper Permian (?) directions of reversed polarity (mean D/I = 221/- 23 °) define a later intrusive event or comprehensive overprinting. The primary Lower Carboniferous pole positions accord with contemporaneous poles from the Midland Valley of Scotland and demonstrate that Carboniferous and younger tectonic movements are palaeomagnetically undetectable, at least between these two areas. Apparent polar wander (APW) movement is confirmed between Lower and Upper Carboniferous times at about 335-320 Ma. directional_or_weak_substitution_warning.excerpt: f palaeomagnetic investigations of Carboniferous to Cretaceous rocks with respect to global-tectonic interpretations of Eurasia. Normal and reverse directions of stable remanence components were found for the Carboniferous to Cretaceous rocks within single outcrops, sometimes even within individual samples. Triassic, Permian and Carboniferous pole positions for Mongolia are strikingly different from those of the Siberian platform. The conclusion about the different palaeogeographical development of Mongolia with respect to the Siberian platform is well seen from differences in palaeolatitudes (up to 500) and palaeorotations (up to 1500). The apparent polar wander paths for Mongolia and the north China block are almost identical since the Carboniferous. This way, palaeomagnetic and palaeogeographical data are contributing to the global-tectonics model of the regions under study. During the Carbonifer- ous, Permian and Triassic, the regions of Mongolia investigated were not part of Eurasia. Together with the north China block, they show a palaeogeographical affinity with the Pacific Plate. 1. Introduction 2. Normal and reverse directions of stable remanence components were found for the Carboniferous to Cretaceous rocks within single outcrops, sometimes even within individual samples. Triassic, Permian and Carboniferous pole positions for Mongolia are strikingly different from those of the Siberian platform. The conclusion about the different palaeogeographical development of Mongolia with respect to the Siberian platform is well seen from differences in palaeolatitudes (up to 500) and palaeorotations (up to 1500). The apparent polar wander paths for Mongolia and the north China block are almost identical since the Carboniferous. This way, palaeomagnetic and palaeogeographical data are contributing to the global-tectonics model of the regions under study. During the Carbonifer- ous, Permian and Triassic, the regions of Mongolia investigated were not part of Eurasia. Together with the north China block, they show a palaeogeographical affinity with the Pacific Plate. 1. Introduction 2. Normal and reverse directions of stable remanence components were found for the Carboniferous to Cretaceous rocks within single outcrops, sometimes even within individual samples. Triassic, Permian and Carboniferous pole positions for Mongolia are strikingly different from those of the Siberian platform. The conclusion about the different palaeogeographical development of Mongolia with respect to the Siberian platform is well seen from differences in palaeolatitudes (up to 500) and palaeorotations (up to 1500). The apparent polar wander paths for Mongolia and the north China block are almost identical since the Carboniferous. This way, palaeomagnetic and palaeogeographical data are contributing to the global-tectonics model of the regions under study. During the Carbonifer- ous, Permian and Triassic, the regions of Mongolia investigated were not part of Eurasia. Together with the north China block, they show a palaeogeographical affinity with the Pacific Plate. 1. Introduction 2. Existing age estimates for the Tortonian—Messinian boundary are discussed; it is concluded that an age of 5.6 Ma is at present the best estimate. Assessment of the magnetic mineralogy in the Falconara section shows that rock magnetic parameters are for a large part lithologically controlled. A second important controlling factor is the numerous joints, which could have acted as channels for circulating groundwater and from which predominantly (sub)recent finely crystalline haematite was precipi- tated, possibly mediated by weathering processes. rock magnetism of the Tortonian—Messinian boundary stratotype at Falconara, Sicily. Phys. Earth Planet. Inter., 71: 100—111. The Tortonian—Messinian boundary stratotype at Stazione Falconara (Sicily) yields normal polarity remanent magnetiza- tions of post-tilting age, implying that the entire section is (sub)recently remagnetized. The absence of direct time control on the biostratigraphic datum levels in the section makes it therefore less suited as a boundary stratotype section. Existing age estimates for the Tortonian—Messinian boundary are discussed; it is concluded that an age of 5.6 Ma is at present the best estimate. Assessment of the magnetic mineralogy in the Falconara section shows that rock magnetic parameters are for a large part lithologically controlled. A second important controlling factor is the numerous joints, which could have acted as channels for circulating groundwater and from which predominantly (sub)recent finely crystalline haematite was precipi- tated, possibly mediated by weathering processes. Component lB compares with palaeomagnetic results from Upper Carboniferous/ Permian dykes and sills in the Midland Valley, whereas HB conforms to palaeomagnetic results from the overlying Lower Carbomferous Lavas. A combination of HB components from the Lower/Upper ORS and Lower Carboniferous lavas (western Midland Valley) yields a relative pole position near S14 and E322 which compares well with Lower Carbomferous data from the Kinghorn and Burntisland Lavas, eastern Midland Valley (S14 and E332). From Kinghorn, the palaeomagnetic data can be demonstrated to be of primary, Lower Carbomferous, origin. Seen in conjunction with the British polar wander path, the Lower Carboniferous poles reported here seemingly dissociate Middle—Upper Devonian and Upper Silurian/ Lower Devonian poles. Palaeomagnetic studies of the Lower and Upper Old Red Sandstone (ORS), western Midland Valley, indicate the presence of two principal remanence components, lB and HB. Both components can be demonstrated to be of secondary, post-Upper ORS, origin. Component lB compares with palaeomagnetic results from Upper Carboniferous/ Permian dykes and sills in the Midland Valley, whereas HB conforms to palaeomagnetic results from the overlying Lower Carbomferous Lavas. A combination of HB components from the Lower/Upper ORS and Lower Carboniferous lavas (western Midland Valley) yields a relative pole position near S14 and E322 which compares well with Lower Carbomferous data from the Kinghorn and Burntisland Lavas, eastern Midland Valley (S14 and E332). From Kinghorn, the palaeomagnetic data can be demonstrated to be of primary, Lower Carbomferous, origin. Seen in conjunction with the British polar wander path, the Lower Carboniferous poles reported here seemingly dissociate Middle—Upper Devonian and Upper Silurian/ Lower Devonian poles. Seen in conjunction with the British polar wander path, the Lower Carboniferous poles reported here seemingly dissociate Middle—Upper Devonian and Upper Silurian/ Lower Devonian poles. Owing to the lack of magnetic age control in the Middle—Upper Devonian data base, it is argued that the majority of Middle—Upper Devonian data from the British Isles should be reconsidered as Carboniferous magnetic overprints. This carries the implication that any tectonic models based on Middle—Upper Devonian palaeomagnetic results should be considered highly suspicious. 1. Received June 20, 1989; revised version received September 27, 1989 In order to shed light on the early Paleozoic paleogeography of Iapetus-bordering continents, samples for paieomagnetic study were collected from middle Ordovician (Llanvirn) volcanic rocks of the Shelve Inlier, Welsh Borderland. The folding within the inlier is constrained to late Ordovician (Ashgill) time, thus offering a fold test with tight age brackets. After stepwise thermal demagnetization, a pre-folding characteristic magnetization component was isolated from 95 specimens. The mean of 11 site mean directions for the characteristic magnetization gives D/I = 116.4/+ 67.9 (k = 89.4; a95 = 4.9°), and the paleomagnetic pole lies at 26.6°N, 36.1° E (Sp = 6.9 °, 8m = 8.2°). The fold test is positive at the 99% confidence level, indicating that the magnetization was acquired during the middle or late Ordovician. We infer from geological considerations that this magnetization is not a primary thermoremanence, but was acquired during late Ordovician time as a result of a thermochemical disturbance of that age. In contrast, no constraining paleomagnetic re- sults have yet been obtained about the origin and evolution of the other major bend of the Andean Cordillera, known as the Huancabamba deflec- tion, situated farther north at 4°S (Fig. 1). The only available paleomagnetic results from the Huancabamba Andes, obtained by our group [6], concern Paleozoic and Cretaceous units from the Amotape-Tahuin massif and the Lancones basin north of the Huancabamba deflection. We interpreted these results in terms of the accretion of an allochthonous continental terrane at Neocomian time, followed by post-accretion in- situ rotation during the Cretaceous. The total clockwise rotation is - 90 ° since the Aptian and -65 ° since the Senonian. Here we give a more complete report of the results obtained from all sites in the Lancones Basin, including a description of rock magnetic properties. port of the results obtained from all sites in the Lancones Basin, including a description of rock magnetic properties. We also discuss the results obtained from volcanic and intrusive formations of similar age situated farther south in the Caja- marca region, in order to compare the sense and the amount of post-Paleocene rotations, north and south of the Huancabamba deflection. 2. Geological setting and paleomagnetic sampling The Lancones synclinorium is situated in northern Peru and southern Ecuador between the Amotape-Tahuin range and the Olmos massif, north of the Huancabamba deflection. In its west- ern part, the Cretaceous formations consist of Albian carbonates overlain by a flysch series of late Cretaceous age. They grade eastward into mixed volcanic and partly volcaniclastic sedimen- tary rocks. These volcanics are characterized by pillow-lava flows intercalated with hyaloclastic breccias and scarce volcaniclastic strata, intruded by dykes and sills of basaltic to andesitic composi- tion. Although not yet dated radiometrically, these pillow lavas are constrained in age to be pre-A1- bian. They are unconformably overlain by forma- tions of the Albian to Senonian volcanic arc and by volcaniclastic series, both of which are intruded by granodioritic plutons

This model suggests that crustal extension during Stephanian to Permian times is responsible for a major fiat-lying detachment. The inferred geometrical relationships between fault azimuth and extension direction is befieved to induce a counter-clockwise rotation of the Paleozoic cover during its northward motion. In order to test this model, we have sampled Autunian (Lower Permian) grey and red sandstone beds within two basins opened during the extension, the Lod+ve and the St-Affrique basins. A first one (A), which is unblocked below 400 o C, is interpreted as a recent overprint due to weathering of the sandstones. The B component is unblocked between 400 o and 575 o C. This B component is assumed to be primary, although the gentle dip of the beds does not allow a fold test. It fits the Lower Permian field direction in the Lod~ve basin

e French Variscan Belt has undergone extension in a comparable way as observed in the Basin and Range Province [1,4]. Associated sedimentary basins of Stephanian to Permian age are locally controlled by single flat-lying detachments (e.g., see Mattauer et al. [5]). In the Montagne Noire region (Fig. 1), the extensional system which separates an upper plate from a lower plate consists of an E-W-striking, north-dipping detachment (Espinouse) and of two oblique transfer faults (Plaisance and Crvennes) which strike roughly parallel to the NE direction of extension [1]. The lower ductile crust of the lower plate is exhumed, forming a gneiss dome: the Montagne Noire Axial Zone. The St-Affrique and Lodrve basins deposited on the upper plate. They are separated by the imbricate units of the Monts de Lacaune. The NE-striking and steeply dipping faults of these units are classically inter- preted as thrusts [6,7]. However, they appear anomalous with respect to the general E-W strike and shallow dip of thrusts observed in the South- ern Massif Central. section_candidates.excerpt: 2, 1990; revised version accepted June 28, 1990 ABSTRACT We present results of a preliminary paleomagnetic study devised as a test of a tectonic model proposed by Van Den Driessche and Brun [1] to interpret the main structural features of the Montagne Noire (South Massif Central, France). This model suggests that crustal extension during Stephanian to Permian times is responsible for a major fiat-lying detachment. The inferred geometrical relationships between fault azimuth and extension direction is befieved to induce a counter-clockwise rotation of the Paleozoic cover during its northward motion. In order to test this model, we have sampled Autunian (Lower Permian) grey and red sandstone beds within two basins opened during the extension, the Lod+ve and the St-Affrique basins. The paleomagnetic study of six sites (three in each basin) using thermal demagnetization procedures, reveals the presence of 3 magnetization components. A first one (A), which is unblocked below 400 o C, is interpreted as a recent overprint due to weathering of the sandstones. The B component is unblocked between 400 o and 575 o C. This B component is assumed to be primary, although the gentle dip of the beds does not allow a fold test. It fits the Lower Permian field direction in the Lod~ve basin

It fits the Lower Permian field direction in the Lod~ve basin (in situ: D m = 194 °, I m = 6 o, k = 50, tilt corrected: D m = 194 °, I m = - 10 o, k = 53). In contrast, it shows a systematic difference in declination in the St-Affrique basin (in situ: D m = 173 °, I m = 2.5 o, k = 101, tilt corrected: D m = 172 °, lm= 6 o k = 37). This is interpreted as a post-Autunian counter-clockwise rotation of at least 20 o of the St-Affrique basin, thus supporting one of the main implications of the tectonic model. Its direction is also consistent with the Permian field direction, showing that hematite crystallisation occurred early in the diagenesis history of the sediments. 1. Introduction After a long period of crustal thickening from Silurian to Visean times [2,3], the French Variscan Belt has undergone extension in a comparable way as observed in the Basin and Range Province [1,4]. e French Variscan Belt has undergone extension in a comparable way as observed in the Basin and Range Province [1,4]. Associated sedimentary basins of Stephanian to Permian age are locally controlled by single flat-lying detachments (e.g., see Mattauer et al. [5]). In the Montagne Noire region (Fig. 1), the extensional system which separates an upper plate from a lower plate consists of an E-W-striking, north-dipping detachment (Espinouse) and of two oblique transfer faults (Plaisance and Crvennes) which strike roughly parallel to the NE direction of extension [1]. The lower ductile crust of the lower plate is exhumed, forming a gneiss dome: the Montagne Noire Axial Zone. The St-Affrique and Lodrve basins deposited on the upper plate. They are separated by the imbricate units of the Monts de Lacaune. The NE-striking and steeply dipping faults of these units are classically inter- preted as thrusts [6,7]. However, they appear anomalous with respect to the general E-W strike and shallow dip of thrusts observed in the South- ern Massif Central. sed version accepted January 4, 1988 A paleomagnetic study of over 250 cores from 26 sites sampled in Early to Late Cretaceous and Paleogene volcanic, plutonic and sedimentary formations of the Lancones basin in the Piura province of northern Peru, indicates that most of these lithologies carry a stable primary remanent magnetization whose direction is significantly different from that of coeval formations of stable South America. A clockwise rotation ranging from 90 ° for the lowermost units to 35 o for the uppermost ones has been documented, although the lack of precise chronology has not allowed a detailed temporal description. Four sites from Late Carboniferous (Pennsylvanian) formations in the Amotape-Tahuin Range also show a 110 o clockwise rotation and yield evidence for a northward displacement. When considered together with previous geological studies, these data are consistent with the hypothesis of the accretion of an Amotape-Tahuin continental terrane to the Peruvian margin in Neocomian times. The accretion was followed by in situ rotation, suggesting a dextral shear regime. These results indicate that the geodynamical evolution of northern Peru is more closely related to the processes observed in Ecuador than to those classically assumed for the Central Andes

sed version accepted January 4, 1988 A paleomagnetic study of over 250 cores from 26 sites sampled in Early to Late Cretaceous and Paleogene volcanic, plutonic and sedimentary formations of the Lancones basin in the Piura province of northern Peru, indicates that most of these lithologies carry a stable primary remanent magnetization whose direction is significantly different from that of coeval formations of stable South America. A clockwise rotation ranging from 90 ° for the lowermost units to 35 o for the uppermost ones has been documented, although the lack of precise chronology has not allowed a detailed temporal description. Four sites from Late Carboniferous (Pennsylvanian) formations in the Amotape-Tahuin Range also show a 110 o clockwise rotation and yield evidence for a northward displacement. When considered together with previous geological studies, these data are consistent with the hypothesis of the accretion of an Amotape-Tahuin continental terrane to the Peruvian margin in Neocomian times. The accretion was followed by in situ rotation, suggesting a dextral shear regime. These results indicate that the geodynamical evolution of northern Peru is more closely related to the processes observed in Ecuador than to those classically assumed for the Central Andes

Paleontological and radiometric data [7,24] indicate that the arc jump occurred between the Valanginian and the Aptian about 130 Ma [22]. The Cretaceous volcanics are mainly located in the Lancones synclinorium, between the Amo- tape-Tahuin Range and the Olmos massif (Figs. 2 and 3). They consist of a basal pre-Albian undated basic complex represented by pillow-lava flows intercalated with hyaloclastic breccias and scarce volcanoclastic strata, intruded by dykes and sills of basaltic to andesitic composition. This basal complex is unconformably overlain by the Albian to Senonian volcanic arc and volcanoclastic series of the Lancones synclinorium [25]. These in turn are intruded by granodioritic plutons not precisely dated but certainly of post-Senonian and pre- Oligocene age [25]. This basal complex is unconformably overlain by the Albian to Senonian volcanic arc and volcanoclastic series of the Lancones synclinorium [25]. These in turn are intruded by granodioritic plutons not precisely dated but certainly of post-Senonian and pre- Oligocene age [25]. One of the initial aims of the paleomagnetic study was to sample the three Paleozoic massifs to obtain a direct comparison of their stable paleomagnetic directions. No suitable site, how- ever, could be located in either the Olmos massif or the Maranon geanticline, so that the sampling has been conducted only in the Amotape-Tahuin massif and in the different units of the Lancones synclinorium. The Ph zone acted as border between Sa and Rh. In the Ph zone, Early Carboniferous NW-vergent thrusting was followed by right lateral strike-slip faulting and Permian Tertiary normal faulting. Within the Sa, Early Carboniferous convergence and Late Carboniferous-Early Permian extension caused predominantly NE SW-trending struc- tures (mylonitic foliations, folds, cataclastic strike-slip faults and normal faults). Intrusions of mafics followed the regional structures. The paleomagnetic results obtained in different massifs of the Variscan belt as Armorican Massif, Central Massif, Vosges, Schwarzwald and Sude- PALEOPOS1TIONS OF THE SAXOTHURINGIAN IN VARISCAN TIMES 11 tians, demonstrate that (1) large-scale magnetic overprints have affected the Hercynides and their environment in the Late Carboniferous-Permian [6-10] and (2) large bloc rotations occurred during the Carboniferous. Carboniferous NW-SE-directed convergence led to the develop- ment of E-W- to ENE-WSW-trending folds with a SE-dipping axial plane cleavage [5]. Right lateral strike-slip faulting along E-W- to ENE WSW- trending wrench-faults outlasted thrusting, espe- cially along the Lalaye-Lubine zone. Deposition of Late Carboniferous-Permian sedimentary rocks and volcanics over folded sequences is con- centrated along these strike-slip faults. In this study, previous results [11] obtained on Early Carboniferous microdiorites, diorites and granodiorites from the Champ du Feu massif and on Late Carboniferous rhyolites related to the Kagenfels granite, are taken into account. It is tempting to correlate this event with the collision of India and the southern Margin of Eurasia which started between M 22 and M 23 (50 Ma) [11,18,19,20], but only became effective in the Tajik basin at about 40 Ma after the contact of the continental margins [19,21]. This is the only major tectonic event in the Tajik basin since Valanginian time. Consequently we must assume that the age of the component B of remagnetiza- tion is from 45 Ma to 38 Ma, taking into account that the subsurface flow phenomena, which is likely responsible for the remagnetization, must have been active before the collision and folding. In this case of a close relationship between a major tectonic event and a remagnetization we have to ensure that the magnetization has not been acquired during folding. In fact, the declina- tion of the Nurek Dam site (324 °) deviates from the mean declination (350 °) after tectonic correc- tion. The directions do not overlap during unfold- ing and the correlation of declination and struc- tural trends (strikes) is negative following Perroud [22]. Geological setting Near the western end of the Himalayan belt, large-scale Cenozoic tectonics are satisfactorily ex- plained by a rigid wedge penetrating into a plastic medium [7]. The wedge corresponds to the north- western part of India, south of the Chaman Fault to the west and south of the Karakorum Fault to the east. This hypothesis is supported by paleo- magnetic results [10], which indicate large rota- tions of opposite dextral and sinistral senses in the eastern and western limbs of the syntaxis. The present geometry of the Tajik basin, which pinches out to the west between the Pamir and the Tien Shan (Fig. 1), is the result of the shortening of the strongly folded Mesozoic sediments of the Peter the First and Alai ranges. Because of the very large number of samples considered in this study, we chose a step- wise demagnetization procedure which could be used almost routinely for all of them: first, the samples were thermally demagnetized up to 330°C (7 steps) in order to completely remove the viscous component, then a stepwise AF treatment was used up to 60 mT in 6 to 7 steps. Typical examples of orthogonal plots obtained by this procedure are shown in Fig. 3. In the very large majority of the cases, the orthogonal diagrams obtained with this method show a perfectly linear trend decreasing to the origin. We believe that the component isolated in this way represent the primary stable compo- nent of the magnetization. This interpretation is supported by the fact that when samples of both polarities are present in the same site, their paleomagnetic directions are exactly opposed which is a good indication of good stability and satisfactory cleaning. Range of eastern Taiwan indicate that, since the late Pliocene, the margin of the Philippine Sea plate has undergone a clockwise rotation of about 30 ° as a direct consequence of the Plio-Pleistocene collision of this plate with the Chinese Continental plate. The rotation is diachronic and started between 3 and 4 Ma ago in the northern Coastal Range then propagated southward at an average speed of the order of 70 _+ 10 km/Ma. This value is in very good agreement with estimates of the southward propagation of the collision between the Philippine Sea plate and the Eurasian margin in Taiwan. It is suggested that the rotation reflects the deformation of the Philippine Sea plate at depth and does not results from the shallow deformations involved in the building of the Coastal Range orogen. 1. This tectonic feature is described as an active thrust [9]. A kinematic model for the evolution of the Taiwan collision has been proposed by Suppe [10,11] on the basis of geological, geophysical and geodynamical studies. We have prefer- entially sampled the fine-grained marls because it indicates that the deposition of the sediments oc- curred in a calm water. The sections too close to major faults or containing synsedimentary struc- tures were avoided. The sampling sites were geo- graphically distributed in various sections, in the different valleys of the Coastal Range (Fig. 1B, and detailed description in [19]). Sampling was done with an electric drill. The corer is a 25-mm barrel with a sintered diamond cutting head cooled by water or compressed air. Orientation of the cores was by standard paleomagnetic techniques using both magnetic and sun compasses. Each core gave 3-5 specimens, 22 mm long. 3. Because of the very large number of samples considered in this study, we chose a step- wise demagnetization procedure which could be used almost routinely for all of them: first, the samples were thermally demagnetized up to 330°C (7 steps) in order to completely remove the viscous component, then a stepwise AF treatment was used up to 60 mT in 6 to 7 steps. Typical examples of orthogonal plots obtained by this procedure are shown in Fig. 3. In the very large majority of the cases, the orthogonal diagrams obtained with this method show a perfectly linear trend decreasing to the origin. We believe that the component isolated in this way represent the primary stable compo- nent of the magnetization. This interpretation is supported by the fact that when samples of both polarities are present in the same site, their paleomagnetic directions are exactly opposed which is a good indication of good stability and satisfactory cleaning. In a general way, it proved impossible to sample both flanks of the structures because the western flanks of the anticlines and the eastern flanks of the synclines are not well developed. Range of eastern Taiwan indicate that, since the late Pliocene, the margin of the Philippine Sea plate has undergone a clockwise rotation of about 30 ° as a direct consequence of the Plio-Pleistocene collision of this plate with the Chinese Continental plate. The rotation is diachronic and started between 3 and 4 Ma ago in the northern Coastal Range then propagated southward at an average speed of the order of 70 _+ 10 km/Ma. This value is in very good agreement with estimates of the southward propagation of the collision between the Philippine Sea plate and the Eurasian margin in Taiwan. It is suggested that the rotation reflects the deformation of the Philippine Sea plate at depth and does not results from the shallow deformations involved in the building of the Coastal Range orogen. 1. Because of the very large number of samples considered in this study, we chose a step- wise demagnetization procedure which could be used almost routinely for all of them: first, the samples were thermally demagnetized up to 330°C (7 steps) in order to completely remove the viscous component, then a stepwise AF treatment was used up to 60 mT in 6 to 7 steps. We believe that the component isolated in this way represent the primary stable compo- nent of the magnetization. This interpretation is supported by the fact that when samples of both polarities are present in the same site, their paleomagnetic directions are exactly opposed which is a good indication of good stability and satisfactory cleaning. Range of eastern Taiwan indicate that, since the late Pliocene, the margin of the Philippine Sea plate has undergone a clockwise rotation of about 30 ° as a direct consequence of the Plio-Pleistocene collision of this plate with the Chinese Continental plate. The rotation is diachronic and started between 3 and 4 Ma ago in the northern Coastal Range then propagated southward at an average speed of the order of 70 _+ 10 km/Ma. This value is in very good agreement with estimates of the southward propagation of the collision between the Philippine Sea plate and the Eurasian margin in Taiwan. It is suggested that the rotation reflects the deformation of the Philippine Sea plate at depth and does not results from the shallow deformations involved in the building of the Coastal Range orogen. 1. Range of eastern Taiwan indicate that, since the late Pliocene, the margin of the Philippine Sea plate has undergone a clockwise rotation of about 30 ° as a direct consequence of the Plio-Pleistocene collision of this plate with the Chinese Continental plate. The rotation is diachronic and started between 3 and 4 Ma ago in the northern Coastal Range then propagated southward at an average speed of the order of 70 _+ 10 km/Ma. This value is in very good agreement with estimates of the southward propagation of the collision between the Philippine Sea plate and the Eurasian margin in Taiwan. Because of the very large number of samples considered in this study, we chose a step- wise demagnetization procedure which could be used almost routinely for all of them: first, the samples were thermally demagnetized up to 330°C (7 steps) in order to completely remove the viscous component, then a stepwise AF treatment was used up to 60 mT in 6 to 7 steps. Typical examples of orthogonal plots obtained by this procedure are shown in Fig. 3. In the very large majority of the cases, the orthogonal diagrams obtained with this method show a perfectly linear trend decreasing to the origin. We believe that the component isolated in this way represent the primary stable compo- nent of the magnetization. This interpretation is supported by the fact that when samples of both polarities are present in the same site, their paleomagnetic directions are exactly opposed which is a good indication of good stability and satisfactory cleaning. In a general way, it proved impossible to sample both flanks of the structures because the western flanks of the anticlines and the eastern flanks of the synclines are not well developed. Range of eastern Taiwan indicate that, since the late Pliocene, the margin of the Philippine Sea plate has undergone a clockwise rotation of about 30 ° as a direct consequence of the Plio-Pleistocene collision of this plate with the Chinese Continental plate. The rotation is diachronic and started between 3 and 4 Ma ago in the northern Coastal Range then propagated southward at an average speed of the order of 70 _+ 10 km/Ma. This value is in very good agreement with estimates of the southward propagation of the collision between the Philippine Sea plate and the Eurasian margin in Taiwan. It is suggested that the rotation reflects the deformation of the Philippine Sea plate at depth and does not results from the shallow deformations involved in the building of the Coastal Range orogen. 1. Typical examples of orthogonal plots obtained by this procedure are shown in Fig. 3. In the very large majority of the cases, the orthogonal diagrams obtained with this method show a perfectly linear trend decreasing to the origin. We believe that the component isolated in this way represent the primary stable compo- nent of the magnetization. This interpretation is supported by the fact that when samples of both polarities are present in the same site, their paleomagnetic directions are exactly opposed which is a good indication of good stability and satisfactory cleaning. Range of eastern Taiwan indicate that, since the late Pliocene, the margin of the Philippine Sea plate has undergone a clockwise rotation of about 30 ° as a direct consequence of the Plio-Pleistocene collision of this plate with the Chinese Continental plate. The rotation is diachronic and started between 3 and 4 Ma ago in the northern Coastal Range then propagated southward at an average speed of the order of 70 _+ 10 km/Ma. This value is in very good agreement with estimates of the southward propagation of the collision between the Philippine Sea plate and the Eurasian margin in Taiwan. It is suggested that the rotation reflects the deformation of the Philippine Sea plate at depth and does not results from the shallow deformations involved in the building of the Coastal Range orogen. 1. lnstitut de Physique du Globe de Paris, 4 place Jussieu, 75252 Paris Cedex 05, France h Laboratory of Paleomagnetism, Institute of Geomechanics, Fahuasi, 100081 Beijing, China Received November 19, 1990; revision accepted February 19. 1991 ABSTRACT Continental Triassic sediments with good fossil control have been sampled in two thick sections (Hancheng, 35.5°N, 110.2°E and Tongchuan, 35.2°N, 109.1°E) from the southern margin of the Ordos basin, Shaanxi Province, China. Detailed analysis of 633 samples coming from 69 sites has been carried out with progressive alternating field and/or thermal demagnetization. Most sites display a low unblocking temperature component up to 200-400°C, which is undistinguishable from the Present Earth Field (PEF) direction, and a characteristic component with higher unblocking temperature with both normal and reversed polarity, which differs from the PEF and later Mesozoic paleomagnetic directions. The pole position from the lower Triassic part of the Hancheng section is at 61.9°N, 348.3°E (A95 = 3.8 °, N = 16 sites). The directions of the characteristic magnetization of the middle Triassic sites from the Tongchuan section pass the fold test and are consistent with those from middle Triassic sites of the Hancheng section, giving a mean paleopole at 59.8°N, 3

A late Permian to late Triassic apparent polar wander path of the North China block (NCB) is proposed. However, a fold test was thwarted by the approximate alignment of the remanence with the axis of tectonic folding. Discussion The positive baked contact test described herein demonstrates that the N1 remanence of the Nipissing sills in the Gowganda area is primary. It was acquired at the time of Nipissing intrusion about 2200 Ma ago, rather than as a secondary overprint during the Hudsonian Orogeny 300 400 Ma later. Thus, N1 palaeopoles which fall in the Pacific near the west coast of South America should no longer be used to support widely accepted polar wander paths for North America that pass through this area at 1900-1800 Ma (e.g. [8,10-12] and Fig. 5). carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: In this study a positive baked contact test is described for an N1 Nipissing sill or cone sheet using stably magnetized mafic dykes of the Matachewan swarm as host. Thus, the N1 remanence is primary and no longer supports the time calibration of polar wander paths which assume that it is a 1900-1800 Ma overprint. 1. Introduction The age of the northerly upward N1 magnetisa- tion which dominates 2200 Ma Nipissing diabase intrusions (sills, cone sheets and dykes) of the Southern Province of the Canadian Shield [1-4] is critical to any interpretation of the early Protero- zoic polar wander path for North America [5]. Nevertheless, the primary or secondary nature of this remanence has long been controversial (e.g. [5 9]). In the present study, a baked contact test was conducted between an N1 Nipissing sill or cone sheet and older Matachewan diabase dykes in order to resolve this controversy. On a widely used version of the polar wander path for North America (e.g. [8,10-12]) the N1 palaeopole falls at 1900-1800 Ma, suggesting that the N1 remanence is secondary and was acquired during the Hudsonian Orogeny, about 300 or 400 Ma after Nipissing intrusion. According to this interpretation, the westerly down N2 remanence observed at other Nipissing localities, is primary. The N2 palaeopole lies near 2100-2000 Ma on this polar wander path. Indeed, a positive baked contact test has been reported for N2 sills of the Cobalt area [10]. On the other hand, Symons [13], Morris [14] and Stupavsky and Symons [4] have reported posi- tive baked contact tests for the N1 Nipissing remanence, implying that this magnetisation is primary and, hence, about 2200 Ma old. These tests, carried out with host sediments of the Early Aphebian Huronian Supergroup, have not been accepted as reliable by many workers (e.g. [5,6,8,10,11,12,15,16]). The scepticism is due to the nature of the palaeomagnetic data described in each N1 baked contact study. 2. Twenty four sites from the top of Sao Khua to the top of Phra Wihan Formation (23 from Sao Khua) are all normal. The Sao Khua samples gave good de- magnetization results, directions of magnetization with good in-site and in-formation agreement (K23, A95 8 for formation), different from the present field direction, and acceptable with confidence (Maranate 1982a,b). The sites are spread fairly evenly through the formation with an average stratigraphic interval of about 30 m, allowing for the possibility of undiscovered brief reversed inter- vals, but not for the rapid polarity alternations charac- teristics of the late Jurassic and early Cretaceous. an. It consists of medium to coarse sandstones and conglomerates which contain some red-bed clasts and we infer unconformity between it and the underlying Sao Khua Formation which consists of fine sandstones and shales, mostly purple-red in colour. Twenty four sites from the top of Sao Khua to the top of Phra Wihan Formation (23 from Sao Khua) are all normal. The Sao Khua samples gave good de- magnetization results, directions of magnetization with good in-site and in-formation agreement (K23, A95 8 for formation), different from the present field direction, and acceptable with confidence (Maranate 1982a,b). The sites are spread fairly evenly through the formation with an average stratigraphic interval of about 30 m, allowing for the possibility of undiscovered brief reversed inter- vals, but not for the rapid polarity alternations charac- teristics of the late Jurassic and early Cretaceous. The age of the top of the formation therefore must be greater than 150 My and, with the fossil evidence, the upper part of the formation must be Callovian (Fig. 3). Pro- visionally we show the Phu Phan-Sao Khua uncon- formity as representing the whole of the upper Jurassic and possibly basal Cretaceous. nges. INTRODUCTION THE FOLLOWING is chiefly a discussion of paleomagnetic data reported by Somkiat Maranate (1982a,b). Other paleomagnetic data from Northeast Thailand (Haile and Tarling 1975, Barr et al. 1978, Bunopas et al. 1978, Bunopas 1981, and Achache and Courtillot 1985) are mentioned also. There are now a substantial number of paleomagnetic measurements from the region, made in various laboratories, and generally in good agreement, lending some confidence to tectonic inferences based on them. SOURCES AND RELIABILITY OF PALEOMAGNETIC DATA Maranate (1982a,b) measured directions and in- tensities of magnetisation in three samples from each of 179 surface sampling sites in Khorat Group sediments and five specimens taken at 5 m intervals from drill cores from Nakhon Phanom (Fig. 1). The Khorat Group has an estimated maximum thickness of approximately 5000 m, ranges from late Triassic to middle Cretaceous, consists mainly of alluvial flood-plain red-beds, and outcrops over most of the Khorat Plateau of Northeast Thailand. The surface samples were taken from six widely separated sections (Fig. 1) and represent all formations of the Khorat Group except the basal Huai Hin Lat Formation (Norian) and its equivalents. It consists of medium to coarse sandstones and conglomerates which contain some red-bed clasts and we infer unconformity between it and the underlying Sao Khua Formation which consists of fine sandstones and shales, mostly purple-red in colour. Twenty four sites from the top of Sao Khua to the top of Phra Wihan Formation (23 from Sao Khua) are all normal. The Sao Khua samples gave good de- magnetization results, directions of magnetization with good in-site and in-formation agreement (K23, A95 8 for formation), different from the present field direction, and acceptable with confidence (Maranate 1982a,b). The sites are spread fairly evenly through the formation with an average stratigraphic interval of about 30 m, allowing for the possibility of undiscovered brief reversed inter- vals, but not for the rapid polarity alternations charac- teristics of the late Jurassic and early Cretaceous. The age of the top of the formation therefore must be greater than 150 My and, with the fossil evidence, the upper part of the formation must be Callovian (Fig. 3). Pro- visionally we show the Phu Phan-Sao Khua uncon- formity as representing the whole of the upper Jurassic and possibly basal Cretaceous. ABSTRACT Remarkably thick sequences of upper Cretaceous and lower Tertiary sediments outcrop on the northern coast of the Basque country. We have sampled the well exposed section along the Sopelana beach over 150 m, spanning roughly from middle Maastrichtian (71 Ma) to lower Paleocene (66 Ma), for both biostratigraphic and magnetostratigraphic studies. Thermal demagnetization of -400 specimens revealed both normal and reversed recent overprints unblocked below 200°C, and both normal and reversed characteristic directions at higher temperatures (200-450°C in the grey limestones; 350-550°C in the redder marls and limestones). Thermal and AF demagnetization and monitoring of weak field susceptibility are consistent with some form of (titano-) magnetite as the main carrier of magnetization. 259 demagnetization diagrams yielded two nearly antipodal clusters of directions, which are still polluted by some 20% remaining recent overprint. The overall mean direction in stratigraphic coordinates is D = 356 °, I = 51 ° (a = 3°), consistent with what is expected for Eurasia at KTB time. Magnetic stratigraphy outlines a succession of eight polarity intervals and is rather straightforward, except for two highly complex zones (52 to 40 m, and 28 to 26 m below the KTB) where the magnetic polarity appea

polarity appears to flip at an unreasonable rate. Biostratigraphic check allows unambiguous assignment of several chrons, with the recognition of the Gansserina gansseri, Abathomphalus mayaroensis, "'Globigerina'" eugubina, Eoglobigerina edita (= E. pseudobulloides) and E. trinidadensis zones. The magnetostratigraphic section therefore begins in chron 31R and ends in 29N. Further detailed study of the complex zones reveals that specimens there have a distinct magnetic behaviour: susceptibility increases beyond 400°C, indicating instability and mineralogical change, intensities are higher than elsewhere and more scattered, and a higher unblocking temperature/higher coercivity magnetic component is uncovered. This component, which is absent from the rest of the section, could be an early chemical remagnetization. Indeed the complex zones contain larger amounts of chlorite, a sign of more intense diagenesis. We have therefore discarded samples showing this anomalous behaviour, and have retained only the 223 samples where demagnetization was achieved by 450°C. About 50% of the Permian samples from the Nammal section contain, hidden beneath a strong recent or Tertiary overprint, a characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM) which is very likely of Permian age. In the lower Upper Permian several normal polarity zones are recognized. This contradicts the current assumption that rocks of this age belong to the long, reversely polarized Kiaman hyperzone. The Illawarra super- chron covers mainly the Lower Triassic and is thought to start in the uppermost Permian. In this study a magnetostratigraphic profile is described which represents one of the most com- plete Upper Permian marine stratigraphic sec- tions. Suitable rock magnetic characteristics and well-determined biostratigraphic control allow for the development of a magnetostratigraphic refer- ence section during the Late Permian. Reliable new Permian data are added here which have been collected in the Nammal gorge (Salt Range, Northwest Pakistan) where marine sediments have been deposited quasi-continuously with occasional minor hiatuses during the late Palaeozoic to early Mesozoic. About 50% of the Permian samples from the Nammal section contain, hidden beneath a strong recent or Tertiary overprint, a characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM) which is very likely of Permian age. This component, which was imprinted on the southern hemisphere, has normal as well as reversed polarity with a normal mean direction (Decl. = 289.3 °, Incl. = -50.3 °, c~95 = 4.3 °, N = 113) which is in close agreement with the palaeofield direction expected for a site belonging to the Indian plate as part of Gondwanaland during the Permian. In the lower Upper Permian several normal polarity zones are recognized. This contradicts the current assumption that rocks of this age belong to the long, reversely polarized Kiaman hyperzone. The mean declination of 80.1" closely matches the declination in Miocene volcanic and sedimentary rocks studied by others in the Western Transverse Block (of which the Santa Ynez Range is a part), and the mean inclination of 38.9" is consistent with a hypothesis that the block was once about 10" south of its present latitude. The combined palaeomag- netic data indicate that clockwise rotation of the block is entirely post-Oligocene; the rotation might not haye commenced until the middle Miocene, or about 15 Myr after northward motion of the block began. Key words: Oligocene, palaeomagnetism, Sespe Formation, southern California tectonics. INTRODUCTION A quarter of a century ago the possibility was raised that the Transverse Ranges in the Western Transverse Block-a region north of Los Angeles bracketed by the Santa Ynez, San Gabriel, and Dume faults (Luyendyk et al. 1985; Fig. 1)-are rotated clockwise relative to the structural grain of southern California (Hamilton & Myers 1966). More recently it was shown palaeomagnetically that the block is indeed rotated clockwise by about 80" (Kamerling & Luyendyk 1979; Luyendyk, Kamerling & Terres 1980; Hornafius 1985; Kamerling & Luyendyk 1985; Luyendyk et al. 1985; Terres & Luyendyk 1985; Ho

ocks of Pleistocene age are rotated by as much as 30" (Levi et al. 1983). On the basis of an inclination anomaly in the Miocene rocks, it was hypothesized that the block was at a more southerly latitude (west of Baja California) when the rotation commenced (Crouch 1979; Kamerling & Luyendyk 1979). Although not fully understood, the structural and kinematic implications of those findings warrant careful examination (Sylvester 1988). The palaeomagnetic investigations cited above were made on Miocene volcanic rocks in the western Transverse Ranges, Santa Monica Mountains, and northern Channel Islands, and on the sedimentary Monterey Formation (Miocene) and Saugus Formation (Pliocene-Pleistocene) near Santa Barbara and Ventura, respectively. Attempts were also made to use Eocene and older submarine-fan deposits on San Miguel Island (Champion, Howell & Marshall 1986) and Eocene sandstone on Santa Rosa Island (Kamerling & Luyendyk 1985) to establish the magnitude of the rotation in the northern Channel Islands. In this research note palaeomagnetic data are reported for the Oligocene Sespe Formation in the Santa Ynez Range that further document the tectonic history of the Western Transverse Block. In this research note palaeomagnetic data are reported for the Oligocene Sespe Formation in the Santa Ynez Range that further document the tectonic history of the Western Transverse Block. Individual dykes may be up to 6 km long by 8 m wide. The dykes tend to dip ESE in the east, and south to SSE in the west, where the greatest concentration occurs. The swarm comprises olivine tholeiites with individual dykes being chemically homogeneous, although they are often texturally zoned with a fine-grained rim coarsening towards the centre. Weathering is confined to a thin orange-brown rind 1 cm thick. Beneath this surface, the rock is dark grey, massive and very fresh. In thin section, the texture is ophitic to subophitic with labradorite, augite and olivine as the major constituents. Olivine is the earliest crystallizing phase occurring as inclusions in labradorite and as individual grains partially surrounded by augite and pigeonite. Labradorite forms laths up to 6 mm, shows polysynthetic twinning and is sometimes oscillatory zoned. Augite is the dominant pyroxene and occurs as equigranular grains. Mesostasis, the last formed interstitial glassy material, in some specimens forms up to 10 per cent of the rock and contains inclusions of plagioclase, magnetite, chalcopyrite and pyroxene. In thin section, the texture is ophitic to subophitic with labradorite, augite and olivine as the major constituents. Olivine is the earliest crystallizing phase occurring as inclusions in labradorite and as individual grains partially surrounded by augite and pigeonite. Labradorite forms laths up to 6 mm, shows polysynthetic twinning and is sometimes oscillatory zoned. Augite is the dominant pyroxene and occurs as equigranular grains. Mesostasis, the last formed interstitial glassy material, in some specimens forms up to 10 per cent of the rock and contains inclusions of plagioclase, magnetite, chalcopyrite and pyroxene. Received 1991 March 25; in original form 1990 December 12 SUMMARY The Kulgera Dyke Swarm consists of olivine tholeiites which have intruded late Proterozoic transitional-granulite gneisses and granites of the eastern Musgrave Block, in central Australia. Preliminary Rb/Sr results suggest that the dolerites were emplaced at 1054 f 14Ma. In addition, a Rb/Sr age of 1060 f 10Ma on a biotite from a pegmatite indicates thermal resetting of the country rock minerals during dyke emplacement. Palaeomagnetic investigations of the dykes yield a primary thermoremanent magnetization direction corresponding to a palaeomagnetic pole at 17"S, 266"E (Ag5 = 12"). In addition to this primary magnetization, an overprint component was present in many of the samples, providing a palaeomagnetic pole at 30"S, 138"E (AgS=24"), which is similar to previous results from other central Australian rocks affected by the Alice Springs Orogeny. The results extend the area of influence of the Carboniferous Alice Springs Orogeny southward into the Musgrave Block. Further, the results provide no evidence for an earlier, Late Proterozoic, Petermann Orogeny affecting the Musgrave Block in the Kulgera region. However, the possibility that a Petermann Orogeny thermal overprint has been erased by the Alice Springs Orogeny cannot be dismissed. Key words: Alice Springs Orogeny , Mu

A study has been made of their magnetic properties, primarily with the aim of determining changes in the palaeomagnetic directions. Titanomagnetite is always the primary ferromagnetic mineral and its magnetic characteristics are common to the various lithotypes. However, the concentration of titanomagnetite and the degree of magnetic anisotropy vary systematically and correlate with the types of magma (basalt-andesite in the first and second volcanic periods; rhyolite in the third and fourth periods). All palaeomagnetic directions are of normal polarity (Brunhes epoch). Their mean overall palaeomagnetic pole (86"N, 238"E; dp = So, dm = 6") is statistically indistinguishable from the geographic pole. The variations in declination and inclination with age, however, are marked by some evidence of a discontinuity between 150 f 10 and 127 f 8 ka. This age can be correlated with the beginning of the Blake event of reverse polarity. The discontinuity might therefore correspond to magnetic excursions which occurred immediately before. Key words:

The first stage resulted in the formation of Panarea, Alicudi, Filicudi and part of Salina and Lipari, the second completed these two islands and gave rise to the still active volcanoes of Vulcano and Stromboli. A transition from calcalkaline to shoshonitic terms over the course of time has also been recognized (Barberi et al. 1973). The volcanic activity in Lipari island took place in four successive periods (Pichler 1976, 1980) and lasted from 223 to 1.4ka (De Rosa et al. 1985). The first two periods (223-42 ka) are characterized by prevailing basalt and basalt-andesite products, the third and fourth periods (42-1.4 ka) by rhyolite or alkali-feldspar rhyolite composi- tions. The first and second periods are marked by strombolian eruptions, the third and fourth by viscous lava flows and endogenous domes (Crisci el al. 1991). carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: ew specimens from each site were progressively demagnetized in steps until a stable direction of magnetization was reached (see Fig. 3). The remaining specimens from the same site were then demagnetized in the field which had thus been determined. For those sites where the direction of magnetization in the specimens continued to change on application of higher fields, several more specimens were progressively demag- netized to determine the peak alternating field at which the dispersion was smallest. For these sites where the dispersion of magnetic vectors was not improved through the above-mentioned AF demagnetization procedure, thermal demagnetization was attempted. That is, the specimens were progressively heated up to the temperature at which their intensity of magnetization was reduced to 5 per cent of the original one or the dispersion of magnetic vectors was smallest. In some cases the thermal demagnetization was more effective than the AF demagnetization to isolate the stable direction. Typical examples of magnetic behaviour upon stepwise AF and thermal demagnetization are shown in Fig. 3 using orthogonal plots. (1) A clockwise rotation of about 45" took place during Oligocene, (2) an anticlockwise rotation of about 75" had occurred since the end of the middle Miocene time, and (3) the Euler poles of these rotations were situated in or near Fiji. A tectonic history of the Fiji region since late Eocene, which can explain the episodes of clockwise and anticlockwise rotations of Viti Levu, is as follows: clockwise rotational movement in Oligocene was closely related to the formation of the South Fiji Basin and anticlockwise rotational movement since the end of middle Miocene was closely related to the formation of the North Fiji Basin. The clockwise rotation of Viti Levu was accompanied by fan-shaped spreading in the northern half of the South Fiji Basin, in which a system, ridge-ridge-ridge (R-R-R) triple junction of plates, was involved. The subsequent anticlockwise rotation of Viti Levu can be explained as 'ball-bearing' rotation associated by antithetical transform faults accompanied with the spreading of the North Fiji Basin. , the tectonic movement in and around the island of Viti Levu with respect to the Australian Plate was estimated for post-Eocene time. The following conclusions were reached. (1) A clockwise rotation of about 45" took place during Oligocene, (2) an anticlockwise rotation of about 75" had occurred since the end of the middle Miocene time, and (3) the Euler poles of these rotations were situated in or near Fiji. A tectonic history of the Fiji region since late Eocene, which can explain the episodes of clockwise and anticlockwise rotations of Viti Levu, is as follows: clockwise rotational movement in Oligocene was closely related to the formation of the South Fiji Basin and anticlockwise rotational movement since the end of middle Miocene was closely related to the formation of the North Fiji Basin. The clockwise rotation of Viti Levu was accompanied by fan-shaped spreading in the northern half of the South Fiji Basin, in which a system, ridge-ridge-ridge (R-R-R) triple junction of plates, was involved. The subsequent anticlockwise rotation of Viti Levu can be explained as 'ball-bearing' rotation associated by antithetical transform faults accompanied with the spreading of the North Fiji Basin. carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: ew specimens from each site were progressively demagnetized in steps until a stable direction of magnetization was reached (see Fig. 3). The remaining specimens from the same site were then demagnetized in the field which had thus been determined. For those sites where the direction of magnetization in the specimens continued to change on application of higher fields, several more specimens were progressively demag- netized to determine the peak alternating field at which the dispersion was smallest. For these sites where the dispersion of magnetic vectors was not improved through the above-mentioned AF demagnetization procedure, thermal demagnetization was attempted. That is, the specimens were progressively heated up to the temperature at which their intensity of magnetization was reduced to 5 per cent of the original one or the dispersion of magnetic vectors was smallest. In some cases the thermal demagnetization was more effective than the AF demagnetization to isolate the stable direction. Typical examples of magnetic behaviour upon stepwise AF and thermal demagnetization are shown in Fig. 3 using orthogonal plots. IC IMPLICATIONS As mentioned in the preceding section, the following conclusions can be drawn from the palaeomagnetic results of late Eocene to Pliocene in Viti Levu: (1) a clockwise rotation of 45" of Viti Levu occurred during Oligocene; (2) an anticlockwise rotation of 75" of Viti Levu has occurred since late Miocene; and (3) the Euler poles of these rotations are situated in'or near Fiji. These rotations must closely relate to the origin and development of the complex physiographical and geological structure in the Fiji region, Timing, amount and direction of these rotations must be important as a clue to the origin and driving forces of these rotations. A tectonic history from late Eocene to present in the Fiji region will be proposed which possibly explains these rotations. amorphism. In Spain the External Zone is generally divided into a number of units which include the Prebetic and the Subbetic Zone (Fig. 1). Pr~ebetic Zone: Due south of the Spanish Meseta, or foreland, and in the northeastern sec- tor of the Betic/Rif orogenic belt is the Prebetic Zone. This zone contains relatively thin Mesozoic to Tertiary neritic and continentally derived sedi- ments in its more proximal reaches and platform facies carbonates with minor siliclastic sediments in its more distal parts. The crust is pa- rautochthonous and was affected in some areas only by a post-Oligocene compression. The char- acter of the deformation in this area has been compared to that in the Jura mountains of east- ern Switzerland [23]. Subbetic Zone: The Subbetic Zone represents a basinal sequence which is the continuation of the Prebetic Zone. This allochthonous sequence was folded and thrust north to northwestward during the later phases of the Alpine orogeny. It is composed of Mesozoic to Tertiary pelagic to deep-water marine sediments. The Mesozoic pa- leogeographic evolution of the Subbetic Zone has been summarized by Garcia Hernandez et al. [24]. along the strike of the zone and across the zone from the more internal to the more external Subbetic realms. The oldest sediments that outcrop in the Sub- betic Zone are Triassic in age. These sediments are comparable to the Germanic Triassic se- quences described from the northern Alps and consist of Buntsandstein, Muschelkalk and Keu- per facies. This Triassic stratigraphy suggests that the External Zone corresponds to a paleogeo- graphic domain that is distinct from the Internal Zone. In early Jurassic time there was a marine transgression. Extensive shallow-water platforms were created upon which carbonate rocks were deposited. These carbonates are commonly at least partially dolomitized. At the beginning of the mid-Jurassic this region began to experience differential subsidence related to the extension associated with the breakup of Pangea. This unit is often referred to as the Penibetics after Blumenthal [22]. The Penibetics are distinguished stratigraph- ically and therefore paleogeographically from the remainder of the Subbetic Zone. Throughout the Jurassic rifting phase this unit never subsided below the CCD but remained a relatively shallow platform. In the late Jurassic, while oolitic lime- stones were being deposited in the Penibetics radiolarian cherts were being deposited both in the medial Subbetic Zone to the north and to the west of the Penibetics, and in the Internal Zone to the south and to the east of the Penibetics. Mor- phologically the Penibetics is a region divided into a series of basins and ranges. The late Juras- sic platform carbonates form the ranges while the late Cretaceous Capas Rojas formation outcrops in the basins. The topographic relationship between the late Jurassic and the late Cretaceous limestones sug- gests that the stratigraphy has been inverted. Paleomagnetic results All the specimens measured were strongly magnetized with natural remanent magnetization (NRM) intensity ranging from 7.25 to 18.40 mA/m. During thermal cleaning, a low temperature component, referred to as the A component, was eliminated below 2000C from most samples. Tri- assic are represented by littoral and shallow- marine clastics and carbonates with intercalated intermediate to acidic volcanics. The Upper Tri- assic is more widespread, consisting, from bottom to top, of non-marine elastics, shallow-marine carbonates, and non-marine clastics with coal seams. Frequent unconformities characterize the sedimentation from end-Permian to Late Triassic times [5]. Conformably overlying the Triassic is a thick redbed sequence of Jurassic-Cretaceous age, which is in turn unconformably capped in places by Eocene to Oligocene red molasse de- posits or Pliocene trachytes and elastic rocks. The Tuoba Formation was described from a type section in the Tuoba area near Qamdo City, about 210 km north of the Haiton section (29.7°N, 98.7°E) where our samples were collected. At the type section, the Tuoba Formation is composed chiefly of blackish/grayish carbonaceous shale, siltstone, and sandstone with coal seams. This succession yields more than 30 plant species, in- cluding Cathaysiodendron acutangulurn (Halle), Lobatannularia multifolia Konno and Asama, Schizoneura manchuriensis Konno, Ptychocarpus (Fascipteris) densatus Gu and Zhi, Rajahia pseu- dohemitelioides Konno, and Gigantopteris dic- tyophylloides Gu and Zhi [18]. The remagnetization of these south China sediments may have an analogy in the Appalachi- ans of the eastern United States. Widespread remagnetization resulting from the formation of secondary magnetic minerals has been recognized in the eastern U.S. and is thought to be a result of the migration of tectonic fluids during the Alleghanian orogeny [19,20,21]. It has also been shown that as two continental blocks collide, hydrodynamic circulation of groundwater is initiated, which may result in the oxidation of pyrite to magnetite and may also account for the formation of secondary hematite [21-24]. Heat from the warm, saline groundwater is now thought to to be one of the major factors facilitating conversion to ferromagnetic minerals [25,26,27]. In the case of the Appalachians, the acquisi- tion of a thermoviscous remanence (TVRM) has also been considered for remagnetized mag- netite-bearing rocks. For comparison, calcula- tions of the stability of a TVRM acquired by magnetite in the middle Jurassic using the ther- mal activation nomogram of Pullaiah et al. Widespread remagnetization resulting from the formation of secondary magnetic minerals has been recognized in the eastern U.S. and is thought to be a result of the migration of tectonic fluids during the Alleghanian orogeny [19,20,21]. It has also been shown that as two continental blocks collide, hydrodynamic circulation of groundwater is initiated, which may result in the oxidation of pyrite to magnetite and may also account for the formation of secondary hematite [21-24]. Heat from the warm, saline groundwater is now thought to to be one of the major factors facilitating conversion to ferromagnetic minerals [25,26,27]. In the case of the Appalachians, the acquisi- tion of a thermoviscous remanence (TVRM) has also been considered for remagnetized mag- netite-bearing rocks. Paleomagnetic studies have been conducted in an attempt to unravel the tectonic history of south China, but nearly all have concentrated on the Yangtze Block [e.g. 7-11]. Few data are avail- able from the Huanan Block. Recently, however, new data have indicated that the postulate of the Hsii group is supported by paleomagnetic results [12,13]. In nearly all of these studies problems with Mesozoic and recent remagnetizations have been encountered. Paleomagnetic studies of three Carboniferous formations from south China were undertaken as part of a tectonic study of the south China region. The samples were taken from outcrops exposed in Zhejiang, Fujian and Hunan provinces on the Huanan Block in order to test the postulate of Hsii et al. l paleomagnetic studies in south China have encountered problems with rernagnetization. The region underwent widespread tectonic deformation during the Mesozoic and the warm, humid climate causes rapid weathering of surficial sediments. Paleomagnetic results from three Carboniferous formations from three provinces in southeast China reveal two possible overprinting ages: one is probably a post-folding Cretaceous remagnetization and the other appears to be a Jurassic overprint which may be associated with the collision and suturing of the Yangtze and the Huanan or North China Blocks. The Jurassic overprint is found in sediments with both magnetite and hematite as primary magnetic remanence carriers. The remagnetization pre-dates deformation in at least one of the formations, further constraining the overprint to the Jurassic or late Triassic. I. Introduction Recent tectonic studies in south China have shown that the South China Block may be di- vided into two smaller blocks--the Yangtze Block and the Huanan Block (Fig. 1) [1,2,3]. The Yangtze Block, which is composed of the Sichuan foreland basin and the Yangtze deformed belt, comprises a single tectonic plate. The concordance of paleomagnetic directions both in different sites from individual eruptive centres and in sites from several different centres, as well as their relatively short age span compared with that of the field as a whole, indicates that these anomalous directions have a geomagnetic origin. The directions, which are dated between approximately 25 ka and 50 ka, do not represent full reversals of the geomagnetic field and are interpreted as excursions. Very few excursions have been reported from the Southern Hemisphere; this is the first such record known from igneous rocks a

Introduction A geomagnetic excursion is a major swing of the geomagnetic field from the axial-dipole field direction. Data on such excursions, which have been reported as occurring over time scales as short as a few hundred years [1], provide impor- tant constraints on models of the geodynamo. However, since excursions were first reported in the literature they have been the subject of much controversy, even regarding their existence [2]. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: was synchronous with a thermal event which affected the older and underlying Finnmarkian-defor- med Kalak nappe complex. Palaeomagnetic remanence studies have proved valuable in dating rock formations and tectonothermal events, elucidating regional tectonic problems and constraining palaeogeographic scenarios. Conversely, the anisotropy of magnetic suscep- tibility, or anisotropy of remanence, can be used to image a rock's micro-fabric and identifying lineations or foliations, pri- mary or tectonic, not otherwise detected megascopically in the field. Magnetic fabric and remanence signature are often unrelated; thus a rock may show primary fabrics whereas remanence can be reset during later thermal events. In this respect, a change in the orientation of the magnetic fabric ellip- soids might require recrystallization, whereas remanence can be completely or partially 'reset' at moderate temperatures without appreciable recrystallization. Anisotropy of remanence studies are important when analysing thermally induced remanent magnetizations (TRM) in an anisotropic rock, a situation often found in uplifted meta- morphic terranes. In areas with diverse fabric patterns, TRM directions would be expected to be deflected from the ambient field direction, resulting in an increased dispersal of remanence directions. Thus, anisotropy of remanence studies might enable the adjustment of TRM directions such that the deflection caused by magnetic anisotrophy can be reversed. C

Anisotropy of remanence studies are important when analysing thermally induced remanent magnetizations (TRM) in an anisotropic rock, a situation often found in uplifted meta- morphic terranes. In areas with diverse fabric patterns, TRM directions would be expected to be deflected from the ambient field direction, resulting in an increased dispersal of remanence directions. Palaeomagnetic remanence studies have proved valuable in dating rock formations and tectonothermal events, elucidating regional tectonic problems and constraining palaeogeographic scenarios. Conversely, the anisotropy of magnetic suscep- tibility, or anisotropy of remanence, can be used to image a rock's micro-fabric and identifying lineations or foliations, pri- mary or tectonic, not otherwise detected megascopically in the field. Magnetic fabric and remanence signature are often unrelated; thus a rock may show primary fabrics whereas remanence can be reset during later thermal events. In this respect, a change in the orientation of the magnetic fabric ellip- soids might require recrystallization, whereas remanence can be completely or partially 'reset' at moderate temperatures without appreciable recrystallization. Anisotropy of remanence studies are important when analysing thermally induced remanent magnetizations (TRM) in an anisotropic rock, a situation often found in uplifted meta- morphic terranes. Circles and triangles are poles determined from the east and west side of the Kapuskasing Structural Zone, respectively. See Table 3 for pole references. Conclusions Since the NB and HSE magnetizations are characterized by both normal and reverse polarity, this suggests that primary remanences have been recorded. The well-defined and charac- teristic Matachewan remanence found in the north-northwest- trending Gamitagama diabase dikes (GD) constrains the mini- mum age of the NB and HSE magnetizations at >2.45 Ga. The results from other paleomagnetic studies of the Matachewan swarm similarly constrain the minimum age for the rest of the prefolding Archean poles in the Superior Province. The presence of both polarities, apositive contact test, precise U-Pb zircon ages, and the concordancy of the NB and HSE poles with the Archean APWP derived from other rock units in other subprovinces of the Superior Province are strong arguments in favor of our interpretation of the ages of the NB and HSE remanences

an granites and Matachewan dikes in the Michipicoten and Gamitagama greenstone belts in the western Wawa Subprovince of the Superior Province, Ontario. Detailed alternating-field and thermal step demagnetization analyses were used to isolate stable remanence directions. A single-component remanence was isolated within three adjacent dated granitic plutons on the eastern margin of the Michipicoten belt, including the Hawk Lake trondhjernite, the Southern external granite, and the Eastern external granite (HSE). The maximum possible age for this remanence is constrained by the intrusion of the last pluton at 2694 Ma. The corresponding HSE paleopole is located at low, 41"s (dp = 8", dm = 13"). A second paleopole, NB, is derived from the Northern external granite and the Baldhead River quartz monzonite, which give U-Pb zircon ages of 2662 and 2668 Ma, respectively. Their single-component remanence defines a paleopole on the Archean apparent polar wander path (APWP) at 15OE, 27"s (dp = 8", dm = 13"), with a maximum possible age of 2.66 Ga. A third paleopole, GD, is derived from the north-northwest-trending Gamitagama diabase dikes and yields a position of 57"E, 41W (dp = 7", dm = 14"), which agrees with poles determined by other workers from the 2454 Ma Matachewan dike swarm. Park (1970) found by X-ray powder methods that hand-picked black heavy-mineral extracts as well as composite grains of red material from two samples from the Maringouin and Shepody formations were composed of a-Fe203. The remanence was probably acquired during deposition or early diagenesis (Tauxe et al. 1980; Tauxe and Badgley 1984). The magnetic stratigra- phy and pole positions obtained from the two formations were probably acquired entirely in the Namurian, beginning with Narnurian A for the Maringouin Formation and completed before the deposition of the overlying Westphalian A Riversdale Group. The intermediate-temperature component (B) appears to be a later (syn-folding) CRM, also carried by hematite, judging by the relatively high (600"-650°C) unblocking temperature. The folding, according to Gussow (1953), is Pennsylvanian (West- phalian B) and followed the deposition of the Cumberland Group (Belt 1965). The magnetic stratigra- phy and pole positions obtained from the two formations were probably acquired entirely in the Namurian, beginning with Narnurian A for the Maringouin Formation and completed before the deposition of the overlying Westphalian A Riversdale Group. The intermediate-temperature component (B) appears to be a later (syn-folding) CRM, also carried by hematite, judging by the relatively high (600"-650°C) unblocking temperature. The present results yield a north paleopole position at 32.

The base of the Maringouin Formation was not seen; the base of the section is placed at its first outcrop along the beach. This study places the Maringouin-Shepody boundary at the first promontory-forming green sandstone. The Shepody Formation, from the first massive sandstone to its upper contact with the Enrage Formation, is complete. Twenty-six samples of the Maringouin Formation and 33 samples of the upper Shepody Formation were taken from the north-dipping limb of the anticline on the eastern shore of the peninsula for fold tests. The Maringouin Formation consists of a discontinuous series of outcropping beds without an upper or lower contact for reference. The sampled outcrop of the Shepody Formation on the north limb begins approximately 150 m from the top of the formation as determined by its contact with the Enrage Formation. The Shepody beds are more continuous than the Maringouin beds on the north limb because of the coarser nature of the sediments. Middle Tertiary studies from rocks farther west in the Coast Plutonic Complex and Wrangellia do show divergences (e.g., Symons 1973a; Hicken and Irving 1977). However, in the main body of the Canadian Cordillera, paleopoles from volcanics and intrusives of mid-Tertiary age and younger are consistent with our result from Stikinia. This is strong evidence that stabiliza- tion and docking of Terrane I and much of the Canadian Cordillera with North America took place by at least the Middle Eocene. Conclusions The Ootsa Lake Group is characterized by a stable, two- polarity, prefolding, primary remanence that was acquired upon cooling when the lavas were extruded around 50Ma. The polarity chrons correspond to 21 normal and 21 reversed chrons (Harland et al. 1982) and provide a useful stratigraphic marker horizon for the Ootsa Lake Group. The Ootsa Lake Group paleopole is statistically indistinguishable from several current estimates of the comparable cratonic reference pole. This tectonic analysis indicates that Stikinia was in much the same latitudinal position relative to the North American craton during the Middle Eocene as it is at present. As pointed out by Kodama (1988), a maximum value of Fisher's (1953) precision parameter (k) at partial unfolding is a necessary, but insuffi- cient, condition to ensure that the magnetization is synfolding in age. Geology The Flores volcanics are composed primarily of welded and massive ash-flow tuff and tuff breccia, with subordinate flows and hypabyssal intrusions. A section of the unit having a stratigraphic thickness of about 730m is exposed on the southwest side of Flores Island. Modal quartz is present in the tuff, indicating a dacitic composition. Chemical analyses have however shown them to be mostly moderately potassic calc- alkaline andesites and dacites, with minor low-potassium tholeiitic basalts (Massey 1989). The rocks were originally mapped as part of the Jurassic Bonanza Group (Muller 1977), but their fresh appearance suggested to one of us (MTB) that they were probably younger. Accordingly, three samples were collected for dating. Fission-track studies (J. A. Vance, unpublished data, 1983, 1986) indicate ages of 51-55 Ma for their crystallization.
